title: Bright Telecom Spin-Photon Interface in Silicon Photonics
authors: Carolina Crosta, Amirehsan Alizadehherfati, Purbita Purkayastha, Kyu-Young Kim, Jasvith Raj Basani, Chang-Min Lee, Fabio Pezzoli, Edo Waks
abstract: Silicon is an attractive host for scalable quantum photonics, but the absence of bright telecom-band emitters with optically addressable spin states has limited its use for spin-photon interfaces. Here we demonstrate the Al1-center, an aluminum--carbon defect in silicon, as a bright waveguide-integrated single-photon emitter with a ground-state spin. Using isotopically purified silicon-on-insulator nanophotonic devices, we isolate individual Al1-centers and observe high-purity single-photon emission with $g^{(2)}(0)=0.04$ without background subtraction. Time-resolved photoluminescence spectroscopy reveals a fast excited-state lifetime of 135 ns, nearly an order of magnitude shorter than the benchmark provided by the well-studied T-center. Resonant photoluminescence excitation measurements further resolve the zero-phonon transition and reveal a narrow homogeneous linewidth reaching 47 MHz, threefold narrower than the T-center under comparable temperature. Through magneto-optical spectroscopy, we resolve the spin-dependent transitions of the bound-exciton manifold and achieve spin-selective optical pumping, fulfilling the prerequisite for quantum state initialization and readout. These results establish the Al1-center as a bright telecom-band spin-photon interface in silicon photonics and introduce a promising platform for integrated quantum networks.
summary: The authors introduce the Al1-center defect as a breakthrough material platform for quantum photonics in silicon. Through rigorous optical and magnetic characterization, they prove it acts as a bright, high-purity single-photon source operating at telecom wavelengths. This establishes the Al1 center as a promising solid-state spin-photon interface for integrated quantum network applications.
main_problem: The use of silicon for quantum photonics is limited by the lack of bright, telecom-band emitters with optically addressable spin states suitable for building integrated quantum networks.
main_result: The Al1-center defect in silicon was demonstrated to be a highly efficient, bright single-photon emitter operating in the telecom band, exhibiting high purity and narrow spectral linewidths.
method: Characterization involved time-resolved photoluminescence spectroscopy, second-order correlation measurements ($g^{(2)}(0)$), and magneto-optical spectroscopy on isolated defects within silicon nanophotonic waveguides.
model_or_system: The physical system is the Al1-center defect (an aluminum–carbon complex) embedded in isotopically purified silicon-on-insulator nanophotonics. It functions as a solid-state quantum emitter with addressable spin states, allowing for initialization and readout.
key_observables: Single-photon purity ($g^{(2)}(0)=0.04$), excited-state lifetime ($\sim 135 	ext{ ns}$), homogeneous linewidth ($\sim 47 	ext{ MHz}$), and Zeeman splitting via magneto-optical measurements.
important_parameters: Telecom S-band emission, $	ext{C}_{2	ext{v}}$ symmetry, fast decay rates compared to T-centers, and measurable spin-dependent transitions.
main_assumptions: The defect structure is stable and its optical properties are dominated by the Al1 center; comparisons are made against established centers like the T-center.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the PL spectrum showing characteristic emission peaks ($	ext{(Al1)}_0$), time-resolved decay curves, $g^{(2)}(	au)$ measurements confirming single photons, and magneto-optical spectra revealing spin splitting.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from identifying the limitation in silicon photonics to proposing the Al1 center. It then presents detailed characterization using multiple spectroscopic techniques (time-resolved PL, $g^{(2)}$, magnetospectroscopy) to confirm its high performance as a quantum emitter and spin qubit platform.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses the hardware requirements for scalable quantum networks by demonstrating a robust, integrated solid-state source of single photons with controllable spin states in silicon, which is crucial for photonic quantum information processing.
